title: What If You Were Born as Miyamoto Musashi? | The Greatest Samurai

paras: If you were born as Miyamoto Musashi, you'd kill your first man at thirteen.
Fight more than sixty duels and never lose one.
And win the most famous duel in Japanese history with a sword you carved out of a boat oar.
But right now?
You're a baby in the hills of western Japan.
No sword. No name. Not even a mother.
You're born around 1584, in a country that has been at war with itself for over a hundred years.
Your mother dies when you're very young.
Some say giving birth to you.
Your father is Shinmen Munisai, a famous swordsman.
He fights with two weapons at once.
Remember that.
And he's not a gentle man.
The story goes that one day, while he's carving a toothpick, you mock his sword style.
He throws his knife at you.
You dodge it.
He throws the next one.
You dodge that too.
So he sends you away.
You grow up with your uncle, a Buddhist monk named Dorin, in a quiet temple.
Chanting. Sweeping. Silence.
You hate the silence.
You're big for your age.
Wild hair.
And you spend every day swinging a stick at trees.
Then, in 1596, a traveling samurai named Arima Kihei comes to your village.
He puts up a sign.
Anyone who wants to fight him, write your name here.
You're thirteen.
You write your name.
Your uncle runs to Kihei and begs.
He's just a boy. Please.
Kihei agrees, if the boy apologizes in front of everyone.
So the next morning, the whole village gathers.
Your uncle starts to apologize.
And you charge in with a wooden staff.
Kihei has a real sword.
You throw him to the ground and hit him until he stops moving.
You're thirteen.
And you've killed a samurai with a stick.
Remember that stick.
At sixteen, you leave the temple for good.
You beat another swordsman, then you walk away from everything you own.
No home. No master. No family.
You're a ronin now.
A samurai with nobody to serve.
In 1600, the biggest battle in Japanese history happens at a place called Sekigahara.
Most stories say you're there.
Nobody can agree on which side.
Some say the losing one.
Either way, you walk off that battlefield alive.
Thousands don't.
And you make yourself a strange promise.
People say that from now on, you'll never marry.
Never cut your hair.
And never take a bath.
Because a bath is a place where an enemy can catch you without a sword.
You're twenty, and you walk into Kyoto, the capital.
The most respected sword school in the city belongs to the Yoshioka family.
They've taught shoguns.
You challenge the head of the school, Yoshioka Seijuro.
You win with one blow.
He's so ashamed, he quits the sword and becomes a monk.
His younger brother challenges you next.
You kill him too.
Now the whole school wants you dead.
They set a final duel, at a big pine tree outside the city.
Their new leader is Seijuro's son.
He's just a boy, around twelve.
And behind him, they hide dozens of students with swords, spears and bows.
But you don't arrive late this time.
You arrive early.
Hours early.
You hide in the dark by the pine tree and wait.
When the boy steps forward, you jump out and strike him down first.
Then you cut your way through the rest and escape into the hills.
Some people will call you the greatest swordsman alive.
Others will never forgive you for that boy.
Quick pause.
A lot of you asked for a samurai, so here's the greatest one who ever lived.
Who should live next? Drop a name in the comments.
And if you want a new life every few days, subscribe.
For years, you wander.
You fight a man with a chain and sickle.
A monk with a spear.
Anyone who'll face you.
And somewhere on that road, you find your own style.
Remember your father, fighting with two weapons at once?
You do it better.
The long sword in one hand. The short sword in the other.
You call it Two Heavens as One.
And nobody can stop it.
By the time you're twenty-nine, you've fought around sixty duels.
You've never lost.
Not once.
There's only one man left that everyone talks about.
His name is Sasaki Kojiro.
They call him the Demon of the Western Provinces.
He's handsome, famous, and he fights with a sword so long, people call it the Drying Pole.
In April 1612, a powerful lord arranges the duel.
A tiny island, between two of Japan's main islands.
Early morning.
Kojiro is there on time.
In his best clothes.
Waiting.
You're not.
You sleep in.
You eat breakfast.
Then you get in a rowing boat.
On the way, you take one of the boat's spare oars and start carving it with your knife.
Remember that stick from when you were thirteen?
You make a new one.
Just a little longer than the Drying Pole.
You arrive hours late.
Messy hair. A rag tied around your head.
Kojiro is furious.
He draws his sword and throws the scabbard into the sea.
You smile.
The story goes that you tell him he's already lost.
A winner wouldn't throw away his scabbard.
He swings first.
His blade cuts the cloth on your forehead.
Your oar crushes his skull.
Then you walk back to your boat, and row away.
After the island, something changes in you.
You stop killing people in duels.
You fight with wooden swords now, if you fight at all.
You never marry.
But you adopt a son named Mikinosuke.
He grows up to serve a lord.
And when that lord dies, Mikinosuke follows him the old samurai way.
He takes his own life. He's in his early twenties.
So you adopt another boy.
His name is Iori.
This time, you teach him strategy, not just the sword.
Iori becomes a top official for a powerful lord.
And he lives.
In 1638, you're in your fifties, and you go to war one last time.
A huge Christian peasant rebellion has taken over a castle at Shimabara.
The greatest swordsman in Japan climbs toward the walls.
And a peasant up on top throws a rock at you.
It hits your leg.
You can't stand up.
Sixty duels.
Not one cut.
And a farmer with a rock takes you out of the fight.
You even write a letter about it.
In your last years, a lord gives you a home in Kumamoto.
You paint.
Ink birds on branches. A shrike on a dead tree.
Some of your paintings hang in Japanese museums today.
Then the pain starts.
Probably cancer.
You know you don't have long.
So you walk into a cave in the mountains called Reigando, the Cave of the Spirit Rock.
And you start to write.
Everything you know about fighting, and about life.
You call it The Book of Five Rings.
A week before you die, you write one last short list.
Twenty-one rules.
You call it The Way of Walking Alone.
In June 1645, you die.
You're about sixty-one.
The story goes that you're buried in your armor, facing the road.
Still watching for whoever comes next.
Your mother was gone before you knew her.
Your father threw knives at you.
Your first son died for his lord, and a boy died at a pine tree because of you.
You started with a stick at thirteen.
You ended a legend with an oar.
And the only thing that ever stopped you was a rock.
People still argue about that morning on the island.
So tell me.
Was arriving late genius, or dirty fighting?
